newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark to hold EU vote in 1998 after court case.
newsitem.headline: Denmark to hold EU vote in 1998 after court case.

text.p: Denmark will hold a referendum on the revised European Union Treaty agreed in Amsterdam in 1998 after the Supreme Court rules in a case challenging the legality of the country's EU membership.

"There is a Danish tradition for holding votes on Europe. We judge that a new referendum on Europe is constitutionally necessary," Danish prime minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen told a news conference in parliament on Thursday.
"Only one thing is certain about the date and that is that the vote will take place in 1998, most probably after the current constitutional court case is over," he said.
Rasmussen said that his Social Democrat-led minority coalition planned to consult the other parties in parliament prior to reaching its decision on the date of the vote.
"The most important thing is that the Danish people are properly informed about the Amsterdam reforms," he said.

"The government will focus on EU's plans to expand eastwards, improved environmental control, efforts to fight unemployment and increased openness in the workings of the union as the themes of the referendum," he added.
"The extension of EU to embrace new eastern European members is the most important foreign policy task in Europe for this generation," Rasmussen said.
A bill of enablement for the referendum will have to be tabled in parliament when it reconvenes in October, but parliamentary sources said agreement on a date for the poll could be announced earlier.
There is broad political agreement among Danish parliamentary parties on calling a referendum on the new European Union reforms and the decision to hold the vote came as no surprise to Danes.

Denmark, traditionally cool towards closer EU integration, threw the 15-nation bloc into chaos five years ago when its voters rejected the Maastricht treaty, which had been agreed in the Dutch town of the same name in 1991.

The Danes accepted the treaty in a new vote in 1993, but only after their government negotiated opt-outs from some of its key aims, notably economic and monetary union (EMU), joint defence, EU citizenship and police and legal cooperation.
Rasmussen stressed that the Danish opt-outs were unchanged by the Amsterdam summit and would remain in force.
The revised treaty agreed in Amsterdam is seen as much less far-reaching than the Maastricht treaty, which laid down the path towards EMU.

Danish political analysts believe there is little chance that the Danes would repeat their 1992 rejection of the Maastricht treaty since the thorniest issues are covered by the exemptions granted to Denmark in Edinburgh later the same year.

Underlining the Euro-sceptical attitudes of many Danes, the Danish High Court completed a hearing last Tuesday on a challenge to the legality of Denmark's EU treaties which legal experts say could end the country's EU membership under the present terms.

After a preliminary High Court ruling on June 27, the case will be appealed by the losers to the Supreme Court and a definitive verdict may not come until after it makes the final ruling at the end of 1997 or early in 1998.

The plaintiffs, a non-partisan group of 10 Danes calling itself the Constitution Committee, argues that since joining the EU in 1973, Denmark has ceded national authority to EU institutions in breach of its own constitution.

Rasmussen's centre-left coalition believes its case is watertight and legal experts foresee a government victory but the result is uncertain and could delay the Danish referendum and final ratification of the Amsterdam Treaty.
